claim: Environmental variability poses a major challenge to any field study.
source: Environmental variability poses a major challenge to any field study.
evidence: This is a general statement about field studies presented in the abstract without specific supporting data in this manuscript.

claim: The ability to detect experimental signals is determined by the degree of replication and the amount of environmental variation, noise, within the experimental system.
source: Thus, the ability to detect experimental signals is determined by the degree of replication and the amount of environmental variation, noise, within the experimental system.
evidence: This is a general principle stated in the abstract without specific experimental support in this section.

claim: A major source of noise in field studies comes from the natural heterogeneity of soil properties which create microtreatments throughout the field.
source: A major source of noise in field studies comes from the natural heterogeneity of soil properties which create microtreatments throughout the field.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact in the abstract and is supported by the experimental findings presented later in the manuscript.

claim: The variation within different soil properties is often nonrandomly distributed across a field.
source: In addition, the variation within different soil properties is often nonrandomly distributed across a field.
evidence: This is supported by the spatial analysis and kriging results shown in Figure 1 and described in the Results section.

claim: Diverse sorghum genotypes and two watering regimes were applied in a split-plot design.
source: Diverse sorghum genotypes and two watering regimes were applied in a split-plot design.
evidence: This describes the experimental design used in the study.

claim: The process provides a method with which sources of environmental variation in field data can be identified and adjusted, improving our ability to resolve effects of interest and to quantify subtle phenotypes.
source: Importantly, this process provides a method with which sources of environmental variation in field data can be identified and adjusted, improving our ability to resolve effects of interest and to quantify subtle phenotypes.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the results showing improved signal-to-noise ratios after adjustment.

claim: Variation in topography may result in uneven water moisture accumulation in experimental agriculture fields.
source: In the context of experimental agriculture fields, variation in topography may result in uneven water moisture accumulation.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about agricultural fields.

claim: Soil nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphate are often nonuniformly distributed across a field.
source: Similarly, soil nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphate are often nonuniformly distributed across a field.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge and is supported by the spatial distribution data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The traditional approach to mitigate variability is through experimental designs that include replicate blocks.
source: The traditional approach to mitigate this variability is through experimental designs that include replicate blocks (Piepho et al., 2013; Fisher, 1925).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: True biological signal may still be masked by experimental noise that is heterogeneous within blocks.
source: While helpful for controlling for variation that is relatively uniform within the blocks, true biological signal may still be masked by other experimental noise that is heterogeneous within blocks.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of traditional blocking designs.

claim: Spatial-smoothing has been shown to effectively account for spatial variations in uniform barley fields and promotes genetic heritability in simulation studies.
source: Spatial-smoothing has been shown to effectively account for spatial variations in uniform barley fields and promotes genetic heritability in simulation studies (Rodríguez-Álvarez et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Estimating and accounting for spatial structure have proven useful for a variety of biological systems including nematodes, microbiomes, forestry, and ionomics QTL mapping.
source: Estimating and accounting for spatial structure have proven useful for a variety of biological systems including nematodes (Quist et al., 2019), microbiomes (Franklin and Mills, 2003), forestry (Ohashi and Gyokusen, 2007; Möttönen et al., 1999; Bai et al., 2012), and ionomics QTL mapping (Pauli et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: In GWAS studies, phylogenetic relatedness is managed by principal component analysis.
source: In GWAS studies, phylogenetic relatedness is managed by principal component analysis (Price et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established methodology.

claim: Principal components capture axes of most variation and effectively reduce a complex multivariate dataset down to only a few independent vectors of greatest importance.
source: Principal components (PCs) capture axes of most variation and effectively reduce a complex multivariate dataset down to only a few independent vectors of greatest importance.
evidence: This is a description of the mathematical properties of PCA, which is established knowledge.

claim: PCs have previously been used for dimension reduction to investigate how various soil nutrients affect natural selection on plant roots.
source: PCs have also previously been used for dimension reduction to investigate how various soil nutrients affect natural selection on plant roots (Murren et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The field study included 24 varieties of sorghum and 2 watering treatments, well-watered and water stressed, arranged in a split-plot design with 8 replicate blocks.
source: This field study with 24 varieties of sorghum and 2 watering treatments, well-watered and water stressed, arranged in a split-plot design with 8 replicate blocks, was completed in 2017.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: Several types of data were collected including plant harvest traits, soil property composition, three microbiome samplings for each plot, leaf traits, and root metabolomic profile.
source: Several types of data were collected including, but not limited to, plant harvest traits (height, fresh and dry weight, and panicle size), soil property composition (calcium, magnesium, nitrate, organic matter, pH, phosphate, potassium, salinity, sodium, sulfate, and total cations), three microbiome samplings for each plot (root, rhizosphere, and soil), leaf traits (specific leaf area, C and N content, and stable isotopes of C and N), and root metabolomic profile.
evidence: This describes the types of data collected in the study.

claim: Only a limited set of points across the field were sampled for soil properties.
source: First, because only a limited set of points across the field were sampled for soil properties, there was a need to estimate the missing values (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Of the 12 properties tested, 6 properties exhibited evidence of spatial distributions (p value <0.05): salinity (mmho), nitrate (ppm), sulfate (ppm), calcium (ppm), magnesium (ppm), and phosphate (ppm).
source: Of the 12 properties tested, 6 properties exhibited evidence of spatial distributions (p value <0.05): salinity (mmho), nitrate (ppm), sulfate (ppm), calcium (ppm), magnesium (ppm), and phosphate (ppm) (see Methods: Statistical testing for evidence of spatial structure).
evidence: This is a result from statistical testing described in the Methods section.

claim: The error of the predictions, when scaled to unit variance of the observations, exhibit distributions that resemble the expected standard Z-distribution.
source: Through this analysis we observed that the error of the predictions, when scaled to unit variance of the observations, exhibit distributions that resemble the expected standard Z-distribution (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the leave-one-out cross-validation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ratio of the partial sill to the nugget is a proxy for the magnitude of the variance that is attributable to the spatial structure.
source: The ratio of the partial sill to the nugget is a proxy for the magnitude of the variance that is attributable to the spatial structure.
evidence: This is a description of a geostatistical concept used in the analysis.

claim: The phosphate spatial correlation was much stronger than the nitrate spatial correlation.
source: Comparing this ratio for nitrate and phosphate shows that the phosphate spatial correlation was much stronger than the nitrate spatial correlation (Figure 1).
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the variogram parameters shown in Figure 1.

claim: Calcium exhibited correlation structure of distances larger than nitrate, but much smaller than phosphate.
source: Calcium also exhibited correlation structure of distances larger than nitrate, but much smaller than phosphate (Figure 1).
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the variogram parameters shown in Figure 1.

claim: The soil properties exhibited different topographies across the field.
source: This analysis revealed that the soil properties exhibited different topographies across the field.
evidence: This is supported by the spatial distribution maps shown in Figure 1.

claim: Phosphate levels were high in a band across the center of the field while nitrate and calcium levels were more variable with several high and low spots.
source: For example, phosphate levels were high in a band across the center of the field while nitrate and calcium levels were more variable with several high and low spots (Figure 1).
evidence: This is observed from the spatial distribution maps in Figure 1.

claim: Several correlation blocks were observed between different soil properties, implying similar spatial structures.
source: We also considered correlation between the different soil properties and observed several correlation blocks, implying similar spatial structures (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in the correlation heatmap in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: All but one soil property, sulfate, showed an interaction effect with the different compartments on the overall microbiome composition.
source: First, CAP was computed and a permutation analysis of variance (ANOVA), using 999 iterations, was performed on each soil property to identify if there is an interaction with the different compartments on the overall microbiome composition and resulted in all but one soil property, sulfate, showing an interaction effect (Table 2).
evidence: This is a result from the permutation ANOVA analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: The root microbiome was invariant to all soil property variations.
source: From this analysis, we observed that the root microbiome was invariant to all soil property variations.
evidence: This is a result from the post hoc permutation ANOVA analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The rhizosphere and soil microbiomes were influenced by the variation in several soil properties.
source: In contrast, the rhizosphere and soil microbiomes were influenced by the variation in several soil properties (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in the heatmap in Figure 2A.

claim: Some soil properties (salinity, sulfate, and calcium) affected either the rhizosphere or soil microbiomes but not both.
source: Additionally, there were some soil properties (salinity, sulfate, and calcium) whose variation affected either the rhizosphere or soil microbiomes but not both.
evidence: This is observed from the differential effects shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Microbiome compartments are differentially sensitive to different types of soil property variation.
source: This suggests that microbiome compartments are differentially sensitive to different types of soil property variation.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of soil properties on different microbiome compartments.

claim: No soil property variances were associated with changes in the metabolomic profile.
source: In contrast to the large effects seen in the microbiomes, no soil property variances were associated with changes in the metabolomic profile (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the CAP and permutation ANOVA analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The lack of association between soil properties and metabolomic profile may reflect the relative stability of the metabolites identified from GC–MS which mostly represents primary metabolites, or the sensitivity of measurements.
source: This may reflect the relative stability of the metabolites identified from gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC–MS) which mostly represents primary metabolites, or the sensitivity of measurements.
evidence: This is speculation about why no associations were found.

claim: Plant height and total fresh weight are influenced by soil phosphate and magnesium variation, respectively.
source: Traditional F-test from the ANOVA revealed that plant height and total fresh weight are influenced by soil phosphate and magnesium variation, respectively (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a result from the mixed-effect model analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Soil phosphate variation is significantly associated with ẟ15N.
source: Similar modeling of the leaf traits indicated the soil phosphate variation is significantly associated with ẟ15N (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a result from the mixed-effect model analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Soil phosphate levels are mildly inversely correlated to plant height.
source: Closer examination showed that soil phosphate levels are mildly inversely correlated to plant height (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown in the scatter plot in Figure 2D.

claim: Excess phosphate inhibits plant growth and development.
source: This supports the hypothesis that excess phosphate inhibits plant growth and development (Shukla et al., 2017; Song et al., 2016) and suggests that the levels found in the center of the field were too high for optimum sorghum growth.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and the observed inverse correlation.

claim: The treatment and genotype effects were accounted for in the first two PCs of soil property residuals.
source: To test the success of accounting for our experimental design, we investigated clustering within the first two PCs and observed that indeed the treatment and genotype effects were accounted for (Figure 3A) as there were no obvious treatment or genotype effects remaining in these PCs.
evidence: This is shown in the PCA plot in Figure 3A where no clustering by treatment or genotype is observed.

claim: The first three PCs represented approximately 66% of the total variance in the soil property data.
source: We selected the first three PCs as regressors which represented approximately 66% of the total variance in the soil property data (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown in the scree plot in Figure 3B.

claim: PC1 is primarily represented by calcium, magnesium, potassium, sodium, and sum of cations.
source: PC1 is primarily represented by calcium, magnesium, potassium, sodium, and sum of cations.
evidence: This is shown in the contribution plot in Figure 3C.

claim: PC2 is primarily represented by sulfate, salinity, and pH.
source: PC2 is primarily represented by sulfate, salinity, and pH.
evidence: This is shown in the contribution plot in Figure 3C.

claim: PC3 is primarily represented by phosphate and nitrate.
source: PC3 is primarily represented by phosphate and nitrate.
evidence: This is shown in the contribution plot in Figure 3C.

claim: The spatial distribution of the kriged first PC resembles the calcium distribution.
source: Indeed, the spatial distribution of the kriged first PC resembles the calcium distribution which emphasizes the contribution of that property (Figures 1 and 3D).
evidence: This is observed by comparing the spatial maps in Figures 1 and 3D.

claim: Larger distances between microbiome compartments were observed using the adjusted counts versus the observed counts.
source: We observed larger distances between microbiome compartments using the adjusted counts versus the observed counts (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in the PCA plot in Figure 4A.

claim: The root microbiome was least affected by soil factors, followed by rhizosphere with a larger separation, and soil being the farthest and most affected.
source: This indicates the sources of variation from the soil properties were better controlled thereby increasing the differentiation between compartments. Within each compartment, the root microbiome was least affected by soil factors which was demonstrated by the small distance between the observed and adjusted counts, followed by rhizosphere with a larger separation, and soil being the farthest and most affected (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is observed from the distances between original and adjusted counts in Figure 4A.

claim: The rhizosphere and soil microbiomes saw an increase in experimental design resolution of 3% and 2%, respectively, after principal component regression.
source: The experimental design was not differentially resolved in the root microbiome after principal component regression; however, the rhizosphere and soil microbiomes saw an increase in 3% and 2%, respectively.
evidence: This is shown in the variance components analysis in Figure 4B.

claim: In the rhizosphere, treatment differentiation was observed using both the observed and adjusted counts; however, the distance between the centers of each cluster was larger after adjustment.
source: In the rhizosphere, we observed treatment differentiation using both the observed and adjusted counts; however, the distance between the centers of each cluster was larger after adjustment further indicating within-group variation was reduced (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the PCA plots in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The variation attributable to soil properties was as much as ±10% for fresh weight and ±6% for plant height for some individual observations.
source: Additionally, the variation attributable to soil properties was as much as ±10% for fresh weight and ±6% for plant height for some individual observations.
evidence: This is shown in the plots of original values versus change in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: Leaf delta δ15N showed an increase in R2 of approximately 5% for the experimental design effects after adjustment.
source: Lastly, leaf delta δ15N showed an association with phosphate (Figure 2C), and variance components for the experimental design effects found that the R2 between the unadjusted and adjusted increased by approximately 5% (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is shown in the variance components analysis in Figure 4E.

claim: Before adjustment on both plant height and microbe abundance of Microvirga in the soil microbiome, there was no evidence of an association in water-stressed samples.
source: We show that in water-stressed samples before the adjustment on both plant height and microbe abundance of Microvirga in the soil microbiome, we do not see any evidence of an association.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4F.

claim: After accounting for the variance from the soil properties, there is a strong positive correlation between plant phenotype and OTU abundance of Microvirga (FDR-adjusted p value <0.05).
source: However, after accounting for the variance from the soil properties, there is a strong positive correlation between plant phenotype and OTU abundance (false discovery rate (FDR)-adjusted p value <0.05) (Figure 4F, G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4G with the change-point model fit.

claim: An order of magnitude more significant OTUs were observed in the change-point associations before principal component regression versus after.
source: We observe an order of magnitude more significant OTUs in the change-point associations before principal component regression versus after (Table 3).
evidence: This is shown in Table 3 comparing the number of significant OTUs before and after adjustment.

claim: Adjusting the soil property effect or other nuisance factors in experimental design can lead to increased power of detecting biological signals.
source: Adjusting the soil property effect or other nuisance factors in experimental design can lead to increased power of detecting biological signals.
evidence: This is inferred from the results showing improved detection of associations after adjustment.

claim: Nitrogen is known to affect plant growth (size, color, yield, etc.).
source: For instance, nitrogen is known to affect plant growth (size, color, yield, etc.) (Veley et al., 2017; Chapin, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: If nitrogen is unevenly distributed across a field experiment aimed at characterizing biomass among diverse genotypes, the variability in nitrogen may confound the experiment.
source: If nitrogen is unevenly distributed across a field experiment aimed at characterizing biomass among diverse genotypes, the variability in nitrogen may confound the experiment.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the known effects of nitrogen on plant growth.

claim: After accounting for environmental variation, a reduced total number of OTUs that correlate with plant phenotypes was observed.
source: After accounting for environmental variation, we observe a reduced total number of OTUs that correlate with plant phenotypes (Table 3).
evidence: This is shown in Table 3.

claim: New 'hits' were observed that were not observed before accounting for environmental factors.
source: While the total number is smaller, we also observe new 'hits' that were not observed before accounting for environmental factors.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of significant OTUs before and after adjustment in Table 3.

claim: Accounting for the environmental variation reduced degrees of freedom that may reduce the power of detecting some associations.
source: We note that accounting for the environmental variation reduced our degrees of freedom that may reduce the power of detecting some associations.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the statistical consequences of the adjustment method.

claim: After adjusting for environmental effect, the analysis focused on conditional associations instead of marginal associations.
source: More importantly, after adjusting for environmental effect, we have focused our analysis on conditional associations instead of marginal associations.
evidence: This is an explanation of the statistical approach used.

claim: Marginal associations measure whether two variables change in the same or opposite directions simultaneously, regardless of other factors that may affect those two variables.
source: Marginal associations measure whether two variables change in the same or opposite directions simultaneously, regardless of other factors that may affect those two variables.
evidence: This is a definition of a statistical concept.

claim: Conditional associations adjust for the impacts of other variables, and measure the relationship between two variables that cannot be explained by other variables.
source: Conditional associations, on the other hand, adjust for the impacts of other variables, and measure the relationship between two variables that cannot be explained by other variables.
evidence: This is a definition of a statistical concept.

claim: Many of the 'hits' before environmental factor adjustment are results of marginal associations.
source: It is possible that many of the 'hits' before environmental factor adjustment are results of such marginal associations.
evidence: This is speculation about the nature of the associations observed before adjustment.

claim: By accounting for environmental factors, the analysis focuses on conditional associations that measure the rarer direct or possibly causal interactions between OTUs and plants.
source: By accounting for environmental factors, we focus on conditional associations that measure the rarer direct or possibly causal interactions between OTUs and plants.
evidence: This is an inference about the nature of the associations observed after adjustment.

claim: The soil property data were collected at just one time point, approximately 1 month prior to harvest.
source: For example, the soil property data were collected at just one time point, approximately 1 month prior to harvest.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the study design.

claim: Some soil properties are expected to remain constant over the course of the experiment, while others likely fluctuate (e.g., water content).
source: While we expect some soil properties to remain constant over the course of the experiment, others likely fluctuate (e.g., water content).
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of soil properties.

claim: Three degrees of freedom were used by including the first three PCs of the soil property data in a regression.
source: In this analysis, we used three degrees of freedom by including the first three PCs of the soil property data in a regression to account for their contributions on the phenotypes.
evidence: This describes the statistical approach used in the study.

claim: Only PCs that have at least 10% variance explained were included, and only up to replication number minus three were included so the experimental design effects could still be estimated.
source: We chose to only include PCs that have at least 10% variance explained and only include up to replication number minus three so the experimental design effects could still be estimated.
evidence: This describes the criteria for selecting PCs in the analysis.

claim: A significant advantage of the method described is that the sources of variation (soil properties) are known.
source: A significant advantage of the method described here, is that the sources of variation (soil properties) are known.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of the method.

claim: The stable isotopes and primary metabolite profiles are invariant to the measured soil properties.
source: We note that in these datasets, the stable isotopes and primary metabolite profiles are invariant to the measured soil properties.
evidence: This is a result from the analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: For the isotopes, the invariance may be indicative of stability relative to the fluctuations in the properties across the field.
source: For the isotopes, this may be indicative of stability relative to the fluctuations in the properties across the field, but it is possible that if the soil property variations were larger, then a relationship might be established.
evidence: This is speculation about why no associations were found.

claim: The metabolite profile used in these analyses is only those captured from GC/MS and mostly consist of primary metabolites such as sugars, organic and amino acids, small phenolics, and fatty acids.
source: The metabolite profile used in these analyses is only those captured from GC/MS and mostly consist of primary metabolites such as sugars, organic and amino acids, small phenolics, and fatty acids.
evidence: This describes the types of metabolites analyzed in the study.

claim: Secondary metabolites that were not examined in these analyses may associate with the soil property variations.
source: It may be true that secondary metabolites that were not examined in these analyses may associate with the soil property variations.
evidence: This is speculation about metabolites not analyzed in the study.

claim: A relatively small amount of variation in plant height and weight were attributed to the soil property composition.
source: We observe that a relatively small amount of variation in plant height and weight were attributed to the soil property composition, other types of data, particularly microbiome composition, were much more susceptible.
evidence: This is a summary of the results comparing the effects on different types of data.

claim: Some microbes were overtly sparse across the samples and principal component regression could not successfully estimate model parameters.
source: Some microbes were overtly sparse across the samples and principal component regression could not successfully estimate model parameters.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the analysis method.

claim: The microbiome table generation pipeline used for this field allows for the identification of very sparse microbes by way of using 99.5% identity clustering which results in 23,617 OTUs detected.
source: The microbiome table generation pipeline used for this field allows for the identification of very sparse microbes by way of using 99.5% identity clustering which results in 23,617 OTUs detected.
evidence: This describes the bioinformatics pipeline used in the study.

claim: After applying principal component regression, approximately 25% of the microbes were successfully modeled and retained.
source: After applying principal component regression, approximately 25% of the microbes were successfully modeled and retained.
evidence: This is a result from the principal component regression analysis.

claim: The methods proposed should be applicable to ASV tables as well, but the percent of ASVs not successfully modeled would likely be larger than if using classical OTU techniques.
source: The methods proposed here should also be applicable to those types of tables as well with one caveat: ASV tables are sparser than OTU tables. While the methods here are zero-inflated, it is likely the percent of ASVs not successfully modeled would be larger than if using classical OTU techniques.
evidence: This is speculation about the applicability of the methods to ASV data.

claim: The microbiome communities were heavily influenced by the soil properties while the plant phenotypes were more resilient but nonetheless affected.
source: We observed that the microbiome communities were heavily influenced by the soil properties while the plant phenotypes were more resilient but nonetheless affected.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Identifying sources of variation and removing their influence enhances the ability to resolve other effects of interest and enables more honest, reliable, and believable quantification of subtle phenotypes.
source: Identifying sources of variation and removing their influence enhances the ability to resolve other effects of interest and enables more honest, reliable, and believable quantification of subtle phenotypes.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the results showing improved signal-to-noise ratios.

claim: A total of 171,273 OTUs were detected from the VSEARCH workflow.
source: A total of 171,273 OTUs were detected and of those 114,179 had quantification across all 1280 samples.
evidence: This describes the results of the bioinformatics pipeline.

claim: After quality control filtering, 92,385 OTUs and 1280 samples remained.
source: After applying this filter 92,385 OTUs and 1280 samples remained.
evidence: This describes the results of the quality control filtering.

claim: Of the OTUs removed, only 422 had counts larger than 200,000 indicating the majority of the OTUs removed were rare.
source: Of the OTUs removed only 422 had counts larger than 200,000 indicating the majority of the OTUs removed were rare and would not have enough information to perform proper statistical analysis.
evidence: This describes the characteristics of the OTUs removed during quality control.

claim: The field trial included two treatment factors (watering treatments and sorghum genotypes) which may have directly affected the measured soil properties.
source: However, this field trial included two treatment factors (watering treatments and sorghum genotypes) which may have directly affected the measured soil properties.
evidence: This describes a consideration in the statistical analysis to satisfy the stationarity assumption.

claim: To satisfy the stationary assumption, it was necessary to account for any influence on the soil properties from the two treatment factors and/or their interaction.
source: Thus, to satisfy the stationary assumption, we needed to account for any influence on the soil properties from the two treatment factors and/or their interaction.
evidence: This describes the rationale for the statistical approach used.

claim: Several spatial models were fitted to the data including No Structure, Exponential, Spherical, Gaussian, Matern, and Stein.
source: The spatial models that were considered include (1) No Structure, (2) Exponential, (3) Spherical, (4) Gaussian, (5) Matern, and (6) Stein.
evidence: This describes the spatial models tested in the analysis.

claim: The best fitting model was selected as the one that produced the minimal sum-of-squares errors.
source: The best fitting model was selected as the one that produced the minimal sum-of-squares errors.
evidence: This describes the criterion for model selection.

claim: The nugget is the estimated variance between two adjacent samples and represents the noise of the data.
source: The nugget is the estimated variance between two adjacent samples and represents the noise of the data.
evidence: This is a definition of a geostatistical parameter.

claim: The range is the distance at which the change in variance with respect to distance first becomes zero and represents how far away sampled points demonstrate the correlation structure.
source: The range is the distance at which the change in variance with respect to distance first becomes zero and represents how far away sampled points demonstrate the correlation structure.
evidence: This is a definition of a geostatistical parameter.

claim: The partial sill is the variance at the range minus the nugget variance.
source: Finally, the partial sill is the variance at the range minus the nugget variance.
evidence: This is a definition of a geostatistical parameter.

claim: Ordinary kriging is unbiased when the sum of spatial weights equals one.
source: More specifically, we applied ordinary kriging and let the sum of spatial weights to be one so that ordinary kriging is unbiased (Olea, 2018).
evidence: This is a property of ordinary kriging supported by a citation.

claim: A soil property is considered to exhibit evidence of spatial structure if any of five spatial covariance structure models are significantly more likely than the intercept-only model using likelihood ratio test (p value <0.05).
source: A soil property is considered to exhibit evidence of spatial structure if any of five spatial covariance structure models are significantly more likely than the intercept-only model using likelihood ratio test (p value <0.05).
evidence: This describes the statistical criterion for determining spatial structure.
